sec:
Vote by mail or absentee

Can’t get to your polling place on Election Day? Here is how to vote by mail in Maine, from the state’s own election office and its laws. Checked October 21, 2026.

Ask for your ballot by

Thursday, October 29Passed

Your request must reach your town or city clerk by the end of the business day on Thursday, October 29, 2026 (the 3rd business day before Election Day). After that, you can get an absentee ballot only by signing a special application giving a reason: you will unexpectedly be away from town the whole time polls are open; you have a physical or mental disability; you live on an island ward or precinct and cannot travel to the polls; or illness keeps you (or the person you care for) at home or in a treatment center. (the law)

Send it back by

Tuesday, November 3Passed

Your ballot must be delivered to your town or city clerk before the polls close on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, 2026. The state's online service puts it as no later than 8 p.m. Eastern time. (the law)

The last day to ask for a ballot by mail has passed. You can still vote in person, early or on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3.You can still vote in person on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3. Early voting in person runs through Thursday, October 29, 2026. When and where to vote early.

Ask for a ballot online, on Maine’s own site

At school away from home, in Maine or in another state? What Maine says about students is under Show more.

Who can vote by mail

Any registered Maine voter can ask for an absentee ballot until the request deadline; you do not have to give a reason. After the deadline, you need one of a few special reasons (see the request deadline). (the law)

How to ask for a ballot

  • Online. Use the state's free Online Absentee Ballot Request service. It is for registered Maine voters living at a Maine address or staying elsewhere in the U.S. for now; it has a separate button for military and overseas voters and one for voters with a print disability who need an accessible electronic ballot. Open it (official page)
  • Mail, fax or in person. Fill in an absentee ballot application, or write a request with your name, date of birth, home address, your signature, and a different address to mail the ballot to if you want one. Send it to your town or city clerk by mail or fax, or bring it in. A close family member can also ask for you. (the law)
  • By phone. You can call your town or city clerk to ask for your own ballot. The clerk checks your home address and date of birth. (the law)

How to send it back

  • By mail. Mail the sealed return envelope to the clerk of the town or city where you live. (the law)
  • Drop box. Put it in your town's secured drop box, which only the clerk can open. (the law)
  • In person. Bring it to your town or city clerk, or have a close family member bring it (they sign for it). Someone else you named in a signed written request can also bring it, but then extra witness rules apply (see below). (the law)

What the envelope needs

Seal the ballot in the return envelope and fill in and sign the statement (affidavit) on it. No notary or witness is needed if you got and return the ballot yourself, by mail or through a close family member, and no one helped you mark it. A witness is needed if someone other than you, the clerk or a close family member brings you the ballot or returns it (a notary, a town clerk, a clerk of courts, or two other adults), or if someone helps you read or mark it (one witness). (the law)

Track your ballot

Track your ballot on Maine’s own site (official page)

Vote early in person instead

Sunday, October 4, 2026 to Thursday, October 29, 2026.

During the 30 days before the election (from Sunday, October 4, 2026, whenever your town or city office is open) you can vote an absentee ballot in person at your clerk's office without filling in an application. Without a special reason, this ends at the request deadline: the end of the business day on Thursday, October 29, 2026. (the law)

Students

At school in Maine, away from home

Maine law says a student does not gain or lose a home for voting just by going to school, and also that this does not stop a student from registering in the town where they live while attending school. So a student at a school elsewhere in Maine can register in that town, or keep their home registration. You can have only one voting residence at a time. (the law)

At school in another state, with Maine as home

Maine law says you do not lose your Maine voting residence by leaving for another state for a time, meaning to come back, and you do not lose it just because you are a student. But if you register to vote in another state, or vote in another state's election, you lose your Maine voting residence. (the law)

Military and overseas

Military voters away from their Maine home and U.S. citizens living abroad can request a ballot through the state's online service (the military and overseas button); the service also links the Federal Post Card Application (FPCA). Ballots must be received by 8 p.m. Eastern time on Election Day. (official page)

Maine in the Federal Voting Assistance Program’s guide

Good to know

  • Maine law lets voters apply for ongoing absentee status, so a ballot is mailed for every election without a new request each time. The published law carries two versions that conflict: one open to any voter, one only for voters 65 or older or with a disability. Ask your town or city clerk.
  • If you asked by phone or online, the clerk will not give your ballot to a family member or anyone else to bring to you (21-A M.R.S. 753-A and 753-B).
  • Someone other than a family member whom you named to bring your ballot back must return it within 2 business days of getting it, or by the close of polls if sooner (21-A M.R.S. 753-B).
  • Any absentee request can name a different address to mail the ballot to (21-A M.R.S. 753-A), for example a school address.

How this was checked

  • The Secretary of State's own absentee pages on maine.gov refused our request, so this record uses the state's online request service and Maine's election laws as published by the Legislature. Your town or city clerk is the place to confirm hours.
Where this comes from: 6 pages of Maine’s election office, its laws and the federal guide

polls:
Polls close at 8 p.m. Each town sets its opening time, between 6 and 10 a.m. (the law)

Anyone in line when the polls close may still vote.
